opus-5.5.text:
I think the cleanest way to see it is to ask what changed when we went from the pre-Transformer era of NLP to GPT. Before, you had a separate model for translation, a separate model for sentiment, a separate model for parsing. Each task had its own dataset, its own architecture tweaks, its own benchmark. Progress was real, but it was local. You got better at task A and that told you almost nothing about task B.

What GPT-style pretraining showed is that if you train one model on a broad enough distribution with a simple objective, capabilities start to transfer. You do next-token prediction on the internet, and suddenly the same weights can translate, summarize, write code, answer questions. And more importantly, when you scale it, it gets better at things you never explicitly trained for. That's the qualitative break. It's not that any single benchmark number jumped; it's that the system started working on tasks outside the training set.

Robotics, in my view, is still mostly on the other side of that line. If you look at what a lot of robot learning looks like today, it's: pick a task, pick a robot, pick an environment, collect demonstrations, train a policy, and it works pretty well in that setting. Then you move the table, change the lighting, swap the object, or put it on a different arm, and performance falls off a cliff. That's the signature of a system that has learned the task, not learned something general about the physical world.

So when people ask "how far along is robotics," I don't think the right metric is how impressive the best demo is. Demos can be very impressive and still be narrow. The question is: if I give the system a new object, a new room, a new instruction it hasn't seen, does it degrade gracefully or does it collapse? That's what generalization means, and that's what distinguishes a pre-GPT world from a post-GPT world.

There are a few reasons robotics hasn't crossed that line yet. One is data. Language had the internet, a huge, diverse, essentially free corpus that happened to already exist. Robotics doesn't have an equivalent. Action data has to be collected physically, it's expensive, and it's fragmented across many embodiments. Another is that the action space and the feedback loop are much harder. In language, an output is a token, and the world doesn't push back mid-sentence. In robotics, you act, the world changes, errors compound, and contact physics is unforgiving.

That's also why I think the interesting research question isn't "can we make one more task work," but "what is the equivalent of pretraining for embodied systems?" Is it video? Is it simulation at scale? Is it cross-embodiment datasets? Is it leveraging vision-language models as a prior and then grounding them in action? Probably some combination. But whatever the answer is, the test is the same one language passed: once you have it, scaling should buy you generalization, not just better performance on the tasks you already had.

So for me generalization is the dividing line because it's the thing that changes the economics and the trajectory of the whole field. Before it, every new capability costs roughly the same amount of effort as the last one. After it, capabilities start compounding. Language crossed that line a few years ago. Robotics, I'd say, is standing right at the edge of it, and the next few years will tell us whether the same recipe, or a different one, gets it across.

r001.rationale: The response describes task-specific NLP models and narrow robotics success, but does not state that fixed-scenario AI success was achievable more than a decade ago.

r002.rationale: It says GPT-style pretraining lets the same model transfer across tasks such as translation, summarization, coding, and question answering.

r003.rationale: It describes robotics as training a policy for a particular task, robot, and environment, with performance falling when the scenario changes.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the clearest way to put it is this: before Transformers and GPT, language models worked, but only on the thing you trained them on. You'd train a translation model and it would translate. You'd train a sentiment classifier and it would classify sentiment. Each task was its own project, its own dataset, its own model. The breakthrough wasn't that the model got slightly better at any one of those tasks. The breakthrough was that one model, trained on a broad enough distribution, suddenly did things nobody had explicitly trained it to do. That's generalization. That's the phase change.

Robotics today looks a lot like NLP in, say, 2015. You can get very impressive demos. A robot folds a shirt, a robot picks a specific object out of a bin, a robot opens a particular door. But if you change the shirt, change the lighting, move the table a few centimeters, change the handle on the door, the thing often falls apart. Each capability is still a project. The model you trained for the kitchen doesn't give you the warehouse for free.

So when I say generalization is the dividing line, I mean it quite literally. The question is not "can a robot do task X." We've been able to do individual tasks for decades, sometimes extremely well. The question is whether you can train one system and have it handle the long tail of situations it has never seen, in the way GPT handles prompts it has never seen.

And the reason this matters more than any single benchmark is that generalization is what makes the economics work. Language models became useful not because they beat SOTA on a leaderboard but because a single model could be deployed into millions of different contexts without retraining. Until robotics crosses that line, every deployment is bespoke engineering, and bespoke engineering doesn't scale.

The hard part is that the ingredients that gave language that generalization don't transfer directly. Language had the internet, essentially free, essentially infinite, and already in the right format: tokens in, tokens out. Robotics has a data problem, an embodiment problem, and a feedback loop problem. You can't scrape physical experience. Every robot is slightly different. And the environment pushes back on you in a way text never does.

So I'd frame the current stage as: we know what the destination looks like, because language showed us. We're still figuring out what the equivalent of "pretrain on the internet" is for the physical world. Once something plays that role, I think things will move very fast, just like they did for language. But until a robot trained in one setting starts surprising us in another, we're still on the near side of that line.

r001.rationale: The response says individual AI tasks had been done “for decades, sometimes extremely well,” and gives task-specific translation and sentiment models as examples.

r002.rationale: It says a model trained on a broad distribution could perform tasks it was never explicitly trained to do, communicating generalization beyond its training capabilities.

r003.rationale: It describes robotics as a collection of individual projects that often fail when settings change, and says capabilities do not yet generalize across settings.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is whether progress transfers beyond the task you trained for. You can make a robot very good at a particular operation in a particular environment. But if you change the object, the lighting, or the arrangement of the room, how much of that ability survives? If you have to collect new data and do substantial engineering every time, you’re still building individual solutions.

With language models, what became compelling after Transformers and GPT was that one model could support many different tasks. You could ask it to translate, summarize, write code, or answer a question without training a separate model for each one. It doesn’t generalize perfectly, of course, but pretraining gives you a foundation that you can reuse.

For robotics, the corresponding question is whether training across many tasks and environments produces a robot that can handle a new situation with very little additional experience. Can learning to manipulate one set of objects help it manipulate objects it hasn’t seen? Can it follow a new instruction by combining skills it already has?

That’s why I see generalization as the dividing line. A successful demonstration shows that a task is possible. Generalization shows that you have a way to accumulate capabilities—and that adding more data and training may improve a broad range of behaviors, rather than just one demonstration.

r001.rationale: The response discusses strong performance on a particular operation in a particular environment, but does not say this was achievable more than a decade ago.

r002.rationale: It says one language model can support many tasks and that pretraining gives a reusable foundation, but does not state that training on one capability generalizes to related capabilities.

r003.rationale: It describes robotics as building individual solutions that require new data and engineering when scenarios change, and contrasts this with generalizing capabilities across tasks and environments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is whether the system can handle situations that weren’t explicitly covered in its training. In robotics, we can already make a robot do a particular task very well in a particular environment. But if you change the object, the lighting, or the layout of the room, its performance can drop dramatically. So a successful demonstration doesn’t necessarily mean you have a broadly useful capability.

With language models, what became exciting after Transformers and GPT was that one model could do many different things. You could give it a new instruction, or a few examples, and it could attempt a task it hadn’t been specifically trained to perform. That changes the development process: you don’t have to build a separate system for every application.

For robotics, the analogous question is whether the same model can go into a new environment, interact with unfamiliar objects, and carry out a new task without requiring another round of data collection and training for that particular setup. That’s why I see generalization as the dividing line. It’s the difference between accumulating individual demonstrations and having a foundation that supports many applications.

Of course, that doesn’t mean robotics has to follow exactly the same path as language models. Physical interaction introduces different constraints. But the thing to look for is that shift: does additional training produce only better performance on the tasks you already collected, or does it produce capabilities that transfer to tasks you didn’t anticipate?

r001.rationale: The response describes robots succeeding at a particular task in a particular environment, but it does not say this was achievable more than a decade ago.

r002.rationale: It says that after Transformers and GPT, one language model could attempt many tasks, including tasks it was not specifically trained to perform, given a new instruction or a few examples.

r003.rationale: It describes robotics as performing well on individual tasks in specific environments, with performance dropping when scenarios change, and contrasts individual demonstrations with transferable capabilities.
